name: Water cutting / dehydration

lead: Water cutting is the deliberate reduction of body water, through fluid restriction, sweating, sweatsuits and saunas, to look drier, leaner and more defined. It is borrowed from combat sports, where athletes cut to a lower weight class before weigh-ins, and is also referred to in bodybuilding for a dry look.

Because sweat is mostly water, weight lost this way is largely fluid, so the leaner look shows within hours and comes back with rehydration. The method is well documented in weigh-in sports, where sports medicine commentary describes it as dangerous.

paras: Methods described include restricting food and fluids, water-loading beforehand, exercise-induced sweating, sweatsuits and saunas, usually timed within days or hours of a weigh-in or photo. The effect is temporary and reverses once fluids are replaced.

Dehydration can cause headache, fatigue, confusion, seizures, heatstroke, hypernatremia and kidney problems. Losses of 15 to 25 percent of body water are described as fatal, and several weight-cutting athletes died in 2015, 2016 and 2017. Some organizations have changed their rules in response.

angle.text: Shedding body water through fluid restriction, sweating and saunas gives a visibly leaner, sharper look within hours, a method borrowed from combat-sports weight cuts. The result is temporary and the method carries documented dehydration risks, including deaths in weight-cutting athletes.

lead: Water cutting, also called a dehydration cut or water manipulation, is the practice of deliberately reducing body water to look leaner or lighter. Physique competitors use it in the last stage before a show to sharpen muscle definition and vascularity, combat-sport athletes use it to reach a lower weight class, and some people in looksmaxxing and fitness circles use sweating, fluid restriction or sauna sessions to look drier, with a tighter face and clearer jawline.[1][2]

Methods described include restricting food and fluids, water-loading beforehand, and sweating through exercise, sweat suits or saunas.[1] A general description of bodybuilding notes that competitors combine carbohydrate loading and dehydration in the final stage to achieve maximum muscle definition and vascularity.[2] The idea is that water held under the skin softens the outline of muscle and facial structure, so reducing it makes edges and veins look sharper for a short period.

Medical references describe dehydration as a deficit of total body water. Mild losses are associated with thirst, headache and impaired concentration, and severe or rapid losses with serious complications.[3][4] Several combat-sport deaths during weight cutting between 2015 and 2017 led organisations to change their rules.[1] Some bodybuilders describe the visual result of a water cut as smaller than expected.[5]

paras: Weight cutting is described as having two forms: losing fat and muscle over weeks before an event, and losing water in the final days.[1] Some athletes diet and add aerobic exercise instead, aiming to improve their strength-to-mass ratio.[1] The practice is used in combat sports, rowing and equestrian sports, where a lower weight is an advantage.[1]

In physique sports, the final-stage routine is described as pairing carbohydrate loading with dehydration for definition and vascularity.[2] Competitors typically also tan and shave before going on stage.[2]

The look sought is a drier, tighter appearance: visible muscle separation, vascularity and, in the face, more defined cheekbones and jaw. Reports from practitioners vary. One T Nation member posted before-and-after pictures from a water cut with a difference of about 15 lb in water weight and described very little visible change.[5]
Dehydration itself is described as producing sunken eyes and dry mucous membranes among its signs.[3]

A comprehensive review of dehydration physiology distinguishes between loss of water from inside cells and iso-osmotic loss from the extracellular space, and discusses assessment by osmolality and volume.[6] A consensus statement from a multidisciplinary group defines dehydration and reviews diagnostic methods and clinical implications.[7]

Dehydration signs include thirst, headache, nausea, reduced urine, confusion and in severe cases seizures. Acute complications include hypovolemic shock, coma, heatstroke and hypernatremia, and rehydrating too quickly risks cerebral oedema.[3]

Reported deaths while cutting weight include Yang Jian Bing in December 2015, Jordan Coe in March 2016 and Jessica Lindsay in November 2017.[1] ONE Championship subsequently banned dehydration-based cutting and moved to a 'walking weight' model with urine specific gravity hydration testing.[1] A Perth physician urged hydration tests before bouts and warned in 2018 that deaths were inevitable without regulation.[1] In 2022 a regulator suspended a fighter for six months and fined him after he posted a video of himself vomiting while cutting.[1]

No studies found of deliberate water cutting for physique appearance. Research on dehydration more broadly includes a 2018 meta-analysis of 33 studies finding that dehydration impairs cognitive performance,[4] a review of cognition and mild dehydration describing impaired attention and memory at about 2 percent loss,[8] and randomised trials of mild dehydration and mood in young men and women.[9][10]

lore.intro: Water cutting comes up in bodybuilding and strength forums as part of peak-week routines and as a way to appear leaner on camera. Accounts vary widely in how much visual change they report.[5]
